title: Common attacks in plain words
summary: XSS, SQL injection, CSRF and broken access control: how each one works on a real app, and the one habit that blocks it.
youWillLearn: The shared root of XSS and SQL injection: data that gets run as code
How CSRF abuses a logged-in browser, and why SameSite cookies mostly stop it
Why broken access control (IDOR) is the most common hole in generated apps
What to grep for when Claude Code writes routes, queries and HTML

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.escape: Turning special characters into harmless text, so the browser or database shows them instead of acting on them.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: an attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your page, in another user's browser, with that user's powers.
glossary.sanitize: Cleaning HTML by removing anything that can run code, while keeping safe formatting like bold and links.
glossary.SQL injection: Input that gets glued into a database command and changes what the command does.
glossary.parameterized query: A query where user input is sent separately from the SQL text, as a plain value, so it can never become part of the command.
glossary.CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: another website makes the browser send a request to your app, cookies included, without the user meaning to.
glossary.Origin header: A note the browser adds to many requests, naming the site that started them. Your server can refuse unexpected origins.
glossary.broken access control: Any bug where a user can see or change something that is not theirs. It tops the OWASP Top 10 list of web risks.
glossary.IDOR: Insecure direct object reference: changing an id in a URL or request and getting someone else's data, because the server never checked ownership.

steps.title: Notely, where anyone can sign up
body: Maya uses Notely, our notes app, in her browser, the screen she types into. Her clicks go to the app server (the computer running Notely's code), which saves and reads notes in the database.
Notes can be searched and shared. Anyone can sign up. Nothing has gone wrong yet, but nobody has checked for holes either.

callout.text: New to Notely? The 4-minute Meet Notely lesson at the start of the Data module shows the whole app, part by part.

scene.caption: Maya's browser talks to the app server, which reads and writes the database.

steps.title: Attackers use your app, not a crowbar
body: An attacker signs up too. Most break-ins on small apps are not clever hacks: someone types odd text into a field, edits a number in a URL, or lures a logged-in user to another site.
Four classics cover most of it: XSS, SQL injection, CSRF and broken access control. Each takes a few lines to block.
changes: + Attacker: a Notely user with bad intentions
~ Holes open ? → 4

scene.caption: The attacker uses the same doors as Maya, with unexpected input.

steps.title: The root: data that turns into code
body: The first two attacks share one root. The app glues what someone typed into something it runs: HTML, the code web pages are built from, or SQL, the database's command language. Typed text becomes an instruction.
The fix is the same idea twice: keep data and code apart. Escape the text, or send it as a separate value.

callout.text: A receptionist reads visitor names over the speaker. One visitor writes their name as "Sam. Fire alarm, everyone leave." Read aloud, a name became an order.

changes: ~ App Server: glues typed text into code
~ Browser steps back

scene.caption: Typed text should stay data. Trouble starts when it gets run as HTML or SQL.

steps.title: XSS: a note that runs code
body: The attacker shares a note with Maya that hides a script. If Notely shows it as HTML, Maya's browser runs the script as Notely's own. That is XSS.
React, which draws Notely's pages, escapes text by default. The holes: dangerouslySetInnerHTML (React's raw-HTML switch), and markdown or AI output turned into HTML without sanitizing.

code.caption: DOMPurify is a widely used library that sanitizes HTML.

changes: ~ Browser: shows the attacker's note as plain text
~ App Server back to normal
~ Holes open 4 → 3

scene.caption: The attacker's note reaches Maya. Escaped, it shows as harmless text.

steps.title: SQL injection: a search that rewrites the query
body: Notely's search glues the search text into SQL. The attacker searches for ' or 1=1 --. The quote ends the text, or 1=1 matches every row, and -- hides the rest. That is SQL injection.
The fix is a parameterized query. The Supabase client does this for you. The risk is SQL you build by hand.
changes: ~ Attacker: searches with SQL in the text
~ App Server: sends the text as a separate value
~ Holes open 3 → 2
~ Browser steps back

scene.caption: The search text travels as a value, so the database never runs it.

steps.title: CSRF: a forged request with real cookies
body: Maya visits the attacker's site. A hidden form on it calls Notely's delete route (the server address that deletes notes). Unless the cookie forbids it, her browser attaches her login cookie. Notely sees a real request from Maya. That is CSRF.
Defenses: SameSite=Lax cookies, no data changes on a GET (a plain link), and check the Origin header.

callout.text: Next.js Server Actions (server functions the page calls) already refuse requests from other sites. Tokens sent in an Authorization header are never attached automatically, so CSRF is mostly a cookie problem.

changes: ~ Attacker: lures Maya's browser to their site
~ Browser: its cookie stays home (SameSite)
~ App Server and Database back to normal
~ Holes open 2 → 1

scene.caption: A page on another site makes Maya's browser send a request. Without her cookie, it fails.

steps.title: IDOR: change the number, get a stranger's note
body: The attacker opens their own note at /api/notes/123. They type 124, and get Maya's note. The server checked that they are logged in, not that note 124 is theirs.
That is an IDOR, the everyday form of broken access control. It is the most common hole in generated apps: every route works when you test with one account.
changes: ~ Attacker: asks for note 124, which is Maya's
~ App Server: hands it over without checking the owner
~ Database: Maya's note leaks out

scene.caption: Logged in, wrong owner. The server never asks whose note 124 is.

steps.title: Fixing it: check the owner every time
body: The route now does three things. It checks who is asking, it queries with that user's own token so RLS (lesson 3's row rules) applies, and it filters by owner as well.
If nothing comes back it answers 404 (not found), not 403 (forbidden), so it does not even confirm that note 124 exists.
changes: ~ App Server: checks the owner, answers 404
~ Database: Maya's note stays put
~ Holes open 1 → 0

scene.caption: Same request, but now the server checks the owner. Maya's note never leaves the database.

steps.title: Side doors: actions and admin keys
body: Every server route and Server Action (a function the page calls on the server) is a public door. Anyone can call it with curl, a command-line tool, without any button. So each one checks login and owner itself.
And a route using the service role key (Supabase's admin key, which skips RLS) leaves your own code as the only check.

callout.text: Grep what Claude Code wrote for: dangerouslySetInnerHTML without sanitizing, SQL built from template strings, routes or actions that read an id without an owner check, the service role key in request handlers, and GET handlers that change data.

changes: ~ Attacker: calls a Server Action directly with curl
~ App Server: each door checks on its own

scene.caption: A script calls a Server Action directly. If the action trusts its input, the page never mattered.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: XSS and SQL injection happen when typed data gets run as code: escape output, sanitize HTML, use parameterized queries. CSRF borrows a logged-in browser: SameSite cookies, no writes on GET, check the Origin.
Broken access control is the commonest: every route and action checks who is asking and who owns the thing.
changes: − Attacker
~ Browser back in view, all doors checked

scene.caption: Same three parts, four holes closed.

quiz.question: Claude Code renders Notely's markdown notes with marked(note.body) passed into dangerouslySetInnerHTML. What do you ask for?

options.text: Nothing. Markdown is plain text, so it cannot hold scripts.
options.why: Most markdown renderers pass raw HTML straight through, so a note can still carry a script.

options.text: Sanitize the generated HTML, for example with DOMPurify, before rendering it.
options.why: Sanitizing strips anything that can run code while keeping the formatting. That closes the XSS hole.

options.text: Move the rendering to the server.
options.why: Where the HTML is built does not matter. If unsafe HTML reaches the page, the browser still runs it.

quiz.question: A route answers GET /api/invoices/:id for any logged-in user, using the service role key. What is the bug?

options.text: SQL injection, because the id comes from the URL.
options.why: The Supabase client sends the id as a value, not as SQL. The real problem is who may read which invoice.

options.text: Broken access control: any user can read any invoice by changing the id.
options.why: The service role key skips RLS, and the route never checks the owner. That is a textbook IDOR.

options.text: CSRF, because it uses a GET request.
options.why: This route only reads data, and the attacker would not see the answer from another site. The problem is that any user can read any invoice.

quiz.question: Notely keeps the login in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie. Which change would make CSRF possible again?

options.why: Lax cookies are still sent when another site simply links the user to your URL. A GET that changes data can be triggered that way.

options.text: Switching the database search to parameterized queries.
options.why: That blocks SQL injection and has nothing to do with which requests carry cookies.

options.text: Rendering note bodies through React instead of raw HTML.
options.why: That blocks XSS. It does not change how cross-site requests are sent.

takeaways: XSS and SQL injection share one root: typed data run as code. Escape output, sanitize HTML, use parameterized queries.
Be suspicious of dangerouslySetInnerHTML and SQL built from template strings. Grep for them.
CSRF borrows a logged-in browser. SameSite cookies, no writes on GET, and an Origin check close it.
Broken access control is the most common hole: every route and Server Action must check who is asking and who owns the thing.
Return 404 for things the user may not see, so you do not confirm they exist.
